entries.content_plain: CHAPTER 26 Ac 26:1-32 . Paul's Defense of Himself before King Agrippa, Who Pronounces Him Innocent, but Concludes That the Appeal to Cæsar Must Be Carried Out. This speech, though in substance the same as that from the fortress stairs of Jerusalem ( Ac 22:1-29 ), differs from it in being less directed to meet the charge of apostasy from the Jewish faith, and giving more enlarged views of his remarkable change and apostolic commission, and the divine support under which he was enabled to brave the hostility of his countrymen. 1-3. Agrippa said-- Being a king he appears to have presided. Paul stretched forth the hand-- chained to a soldier ( Ac 26:29 , and see on Ac 12:6 ).

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16252"/><div sID="gen31441" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16252"/><hi type="bold">8. Why should it be thought a thing incredible ... that God should raise the dead?--</hi>rather, "Why is it judged a thing incredible if God raises the dead?" the case being viewed as an accomplished fact. No one dared to call in question the overwhelming evidence of the resurrection of Jesus, which proclaimed Him to be the Christ, the Son of God; the only way of getting rid of it, therefore, was to pronounce it incredible. But why, asks the apostle, is it so judged? Leaving this pregnant question to find its answer in the breasts of his audience, he now passes to his personal history. <div eID="gen31441" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16254"/><div sID="gen31443" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16254"/><hi type="bold">16-18. But rise, &c.--</hi>Here the apostle appears to condense into one statement various sayings of his Lord to him in visions at different times, in order to present at one view the grandeur of the commission with which his Master had clothed him [Alford].<div eID="gen31443" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31444" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a minister ... both of these things which thou hast seen--</hi>putting him on a footing with those "eye-witnesses and ministers of the word" mentioned in <reference osisRef="Luke.1.2">Lu 1:2</reference>.<div eID="gen31444" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31445" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and of those in which I will appear to thee--</hi>referring to visions he was thereafter to be favored with; such as <reference osisRef="Acts.18.9">Ac 18:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.18.10">10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.22.17-Acts.22.21">22:17-21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.23.11">23:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.1-2Cor.12.10">2Co 12:1-10</reference>, &c. (<reference osisRef="Gal.1.12">Ga 1:12</reference>). <div eID="gen31445" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 16-18. But rise, &c.-- Here the apostle appears to condense into one statement various sayings of his Lord to him in visions at different times, in order to present at one view the grandeur of the commission with which his Master had clothed him [Alford]. a minister ... both of these things which thou hast seen-- putting him on a footing with those "eye-witnesses and ministers of the word" mentioned in Lu 1:2 . and of those in which I will appear to thee-- referring to visions he was thereafter to be favored with; such as Ac 18:9 , 10 ; 22:17-21 ; 23:11 ; 2Co 12:1-10 , &c. ( Ga 1:12 ).

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16261"/><div sID="gen31460" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16261"/><hi type="bold">24. Festus said with a loud voice--</hi>surprised and bewildered.<div eID="gen31460" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31461" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Paul, thou art beside thyself, much learning doth make thee mad--</hi>"is turning thy head." The union of flowing Greek, deep acquaintance with the sacred writings of his nation, reference to a resurrection and other doctrines to a Roman utterly unintelligible, and, above all, lofty religious earnestness, so strange to the cultivated, cold-hearted skeptics of that day--may account for this sudden exclamation. <div eID="gen31461" type="x-p"/>
